quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Which is more convincing: 'Our tutoring service really helps kids improve,' or 'Kids move up a full reading level after eight weeks with us.' Pick one and explain why.
quests.correctAnswer: The second - a specific, concrete claim is easier to believe than a vague one, even without a fancy statistic behind it.
quests.hint: Ask which sentence a skeptical parent could actually picture happening.
quests.explanation: Concreteness builds trust faster than enthusiasm does. Specific, plausible detail feels more honest than a general claim.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: This pitch is too abstract: 'Our budgeting app makes managing money easier.' Make it concrete by describing one specific moment it helps with.
quests.correctAnswer: The night before rent is due, it shows you exactly what you can safely spend without checking your account five times.
quests.hint: Picture one specific moment where the vague claim becomes real.
quests.explanation: One vivid, specific moment does more work than three abstract adjectives stacked together.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Now take a vague personal claim - 'I'm good at solving problems under pressure' - and turn it concrete for a job interview.
quests.correctAnswer: When our server crashed an hour before a client demo, I rerouted the whole presentation onto a backup laptop in under ten minutes.
quests.hint: Trade the adjective for a specific moment where it was actually true.
quests.explanation: Concrete beats abstract for self-pitches too - a real example proves the trait instead of just claiming it.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Compare two openings for a pitch about a recycling startup: 'We're a sustainability-focused recycling solution,' versus 'Every coffee cup you've ever thrown away is probably still in a landfill somewhere.' Which is a stronger hook, and why?
quests.correctAnswer: The second - it puts a specific, slightly uncomfortable image in the listener's head before asking anything of them.
quests.hint: A hook should make the listener curious, not summarize your company.
quests.explanation: A strong opening creates a small gap the listener wants closed - a label just states a category and closes nothing.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Write a memorable opening line for a pitch about an app that helps people find lost pets faster.
quests.correctAnswer: The first hour after a pet goes missing matters more than the next ten combined - most people don't know that until it's too late.
quests.hint: Open with a surprising fact or moment, not with 'our app is.'
quests.explanation: A hook earns the next sentence. If the opening doesn't create curiosity, the rest of the pitch has to work twice as hard.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Now write a hook-style opening for introducing yourself at a networking event, without saying your job title first.
quests.correctAnswer: I spend my days convincing strict spreadsheets to tell honest stories - I'm an analyst, but that's the boring part.
quests.hint: Start with what you actually do in practice, save the title for the payoff.
quests.explanation: Delaying the job title slightly, in favor of what the work actually feels like, is a simple way to make a self-introduction memorable.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A pitch that's all beginning - hook, hook, hook, no payoff - leaves the listener with what problem?
quests.correctAnswer: They're curious but never actually told what's being offered or why it matters to them.
quests.hint: Think about what happens if a pitch never moves past the opening line.
quests.explanation: A hook opens a gap; the middle and end have to close it, or the pitch never actually delivers anything.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Here's a pitch with only a beginning: 'Imagine never losing a receipt again.' Add a middle (what it is) and an end (the payoff) to complete it.
quests.correctAnswer: Imagine never losing a receipt again. Our app photographs and organizes every receipt the second you get it, so tax season becomes a five-minute job instead of a weekend one.
quests.hint: Middle explains what it is, end delivers the concrete payoff.
quests.explanation: A complete pitch moves the listener from curiosity to understanding to a reason to care, in that order.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Apply the same beginning-middle-end structure to pitch a community skill-swap event, where a piano teacher trades lessons for someone else's home repairs.
quests.correctAnswer: What if the thing you're best at could pay for the thing you're worst at? At our skill-swap night, neighbors trade an hour of their expertise for someone else's - no money changes hands, just useful skills.
quests.hint: Start with a question or image, explain the mechanism, end with the concrete result.
quests.explanation: The structure is portable across completely different ideas once you've internalized what each part is doing.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Which ending is stronger for a pitch: 'So yeah, that's basically it, anyway,' or 'That's the whole idea - and it starts with one photo.' Choose and explain.
quests.correctAnswer: The second - it restates the core idea with energy and gives the listener something concrete to picture as it ends.
quests.hint: A weak ending trails off. A strong one leaves the listener with one clear image or next step.
quests.explanation: The last sentence is what a listener remembers most, so it deserves as much care as the opening line.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: This pitch has a strong middle but a weak ending: 'So basically that's the gist of it, I think.' Replace the ending with something stronger, keeping the same idea.
quests.correctAnswer: That's the app in one sentence: it remembers your medication so you don't have to.
quests.hint: End with a compact restatement of the core value, not a trailing apology.
quests.explanation: A strong close often mirrors the opening idea in fewer words - it feels like the pitch is landing, not fading out.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Write a strong closing line for a pitch about a freelance web-design service, ending on the listener's next possible action.
quests.correctAnswer: If your website is quietly costing you customers, let's find out in a fifteen-minute call this week.
quests.hint: End on something the listener could actually do next, not just a summary.
quests.explanation: Ending on a small, concrete next step turns a pitch from a monologue into the start of an actual conversation.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: What's missing from this pitch as a value proposition: 'We built a really cool app with a lot of features'? Identify the gap.
quests.correctAnswer: It never says who the app is for or what specific problem it solves - 'cool' and 'a lot of features' aren't a value proposition.
quests.hint: A value proposition needs a who, a what problem, and a why-better - check which of those are present.
quests.explanation: 'Cool' is an opinion. A value proposition is a claim a listener can test against their own situation.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Turn this into a real value proposition: 'Our app has a lot of features for managing your time.' Say specifically who it's for and what changes for them.
quests.correctAnswer: For freelancers juggling five clients at once, it turns a messy week into one clear schedule you can actually trust.
quests.hint: Name the specific audience and the specific change, not just 'time management.'
quests.explanation: A value proposition gets sharper the more specific the audience and the change become - vague audiences produce vague value.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Write a value proposition for a local bakery that only sells bread made with a two-day fermentation process, aimed at a customer who's never heard of that term.
quests.correctAnswer: Bread that's given two full days to develop flavor, instead of two hours, tastes like something your grandmother might have made.
quests.hint: Translate the technical process into a comparison the listener already understands.
quests.explanation: Translating an unfamiliar process into a familiar comparison is often what turns technical accuracy into actual persuasion.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: 'Our software has advanced encryption' is a feature statement. What outcome could it be translated into for a small business owner?
quests.correctAnswer: Your customers' payment details stay safe, even if your laptop gets stolen tomorrow.
quests.hint: Ask what the encryption actually protects the listener from, in plain terms.
quests.explanation: Outcome language answers 'so what happens to me' - a feature alone leaves that question unanswered.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Rewrite this feature-heavy pitch into outcome-focused language: 'Our app has cloud sync, offline mode, and automatic backups.'
quests.correctAnswer: Lose your phone tomorrow, and every note you've ever taken is still there the moment you log in on a new one.
quests.hint: Pick the single outcome all three features add up to, and lead with that.
quests.explanation: Three features can often collapse into one outcome - finding that outcome is more useful than listing all three.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A personal trainer wants to stop saying 'I create customized twelve-week programs' and start speaking in outcomes. Write the outcome-focused version.
quests.correctAnswer: By week twelve, you're not guessing at the gym anymore - you know exactly what to do and you're actually seeing it work.
quests.hint: Describe what's different for the client at the end, not the structure of the service.
quests.explanation: Even service-based pitches benefit from outcome language - clients buy a future state, not a method.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Which claim is more persuasive: 'Our course helps you learn a language fast,' or 'Our course gets you ordering food and asking directions in three weeks.' Choose and explain.
quests.correctAnswer: The second - 'fast' is vague, but 'ordering food and asking directions in three weeks' is a specific, checkable promise.
quests.hint: Vague claims ask for trust. Specific claims let the listener judge for themselves.
quests.explanation: Specificity works because it's falsifiable - a listener can imagine testing it, which paradoxically makes it more believable.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Make this claim more specific: 'Our cleaning service does a really thorough job.' Give one concrete detail that proves thoroughness.
quests.correctAnswer: We move the couch and vacuum underneath it - most services skip that entirely.
quests.hint: Name one specific action most competitors skip, instead of a general adjective.
quests.explanation: One specific, checkable detail proves a general claim far better than repeating the adjective more emphatically.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Pitch a resume-writing service using at least one specific, concrete detail rather than general claims about quality.
quests.correctAnswer: We rewrite your bullet points around actual numbers - 'managed a team' becomes 'led six people to cut turnaround time by a third.'
quests.hint: Show the specific transformation, not just a promise that it will be better.
quests.explanation: Showing the actual before-and-after of a transformation is more convincing than promising a vague improvement.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: This pitch drowns its point in detail: 'Our app, available on both iOS and Android, uses a proprietary algorithm built over eighteen months by our four-person engineering team, to recommend recipes.' What single sentence is actually needed?
quests.correctAnswer: Our app recommends recipes based on what's already in your fridge, so nothing goes to waste.
quests.hint: Ask what the listener needs to know to decide if they're interested - nothing more.
quests.explanation: Every detail you add costs attention. Cutting to the one sentence that matters isn't losing information, it's protecting the point.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Trim this pitch down to its essential sentence: 'We're a three-person team based out of a small office, and what we do, after a lot of research and testing, is help small restaurants manage their online reviews more effectively.'
quests.correctAnswer: We help small restaurants turn scattered online reviews into a plan they can actually act on.
quests.hint: Cut the team size, office, and research history - keep only what the pitch is.
quests.explanation: A listener rarely needs your operational history to evaluate whether your idea is relevant to them.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: You have ten seconds, not thirty, to pitch a car-sharing app to someone at a bus stop. Cut everything down to the single most essential sentence.
quests.correctAnswer: Rent the neighbor's car by the hour, cheaper than owning one you barely drive.
quests.hint: Imagine the words disappearing one by one until only the core claim survives.
quests.explanation: Extreme time pressure is a useful test - whatever survives being cut to ten seconds is usually the real core of the pitch.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Your app has three true selling points: it's cheaper than competitors, it's faster to set up, and it has better customer support. For a first-time small business owner, which should lead, and why?
quests.correctAnswer: Faster to set up - a first-time owner is more worried about not knowing how to get started than about price or support they haven't needed yet.
quests.hint: Match the message to what this specific listener is most likely anxious about right now.
quests.explanation: When several claims are all true, choosing which one leads is itself a communication skill - the right choice depends entirely on the listener.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Now pitch the same app to an existing business owner switching from a competitor, choosing a different one of those three true points to lead with.
quests.correctAnswer: Support that actually answers the phone - if you've ever been stuck on hold with your current provider, that's the whole reason to switch.
quests.hint: This listener already knows how to set up software - lead with whatever pain they're most likely already feeling.
quests.explanation: The same three true facts can each be the right lead, depending entirely on which listener you're in front of.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A friend has to choose one thing to lead with when introducing themselves at two different interviews: one at a startup, one at a large bank. They're both a strong coder and a strong communicator. Advise them on the split.
quests.correctAnswer: Lead with communication at the startup, where everyone already assumes you can code but few can explain decisions clearly; lead with the coding depth at the bank, where technical rigor is what gets questioned first.
quests.hint: Ask which trait is rarer or more in doubt in each specific room.
quests.explanation: Choosing what to lead with is about what's scarce or in question for that listener, not about which trait you're proudest of.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: You've just built a simple app that lets apartment neighbors split a single high-speed internet bill instead of each paying for their own. Build the opening hook only - one sentence that would make a neighbor stop and listen.
quests.correctAnswer: What if the five of you on this floor have been paying for five separate internet bills this whole time?
quests.hint: Use a surprising, specific fact rather than a category label.
quests.explanation: By now you've practiced every piece separately - this level asks you to apply just the opening skill cleanly, under real constraints.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Take that same internet-splitting app and write the complete pitch: hook, the problem, the solution, and a clear close, in three or four sentences total.
quests.correctAnswer: What if the five of you on this floor have been paying for five separate internet bills this whole time? One shared connection, split automatically and fairly every month, costs each of you a fraction of what you're paying now. No more juggling five different providers. Want to see what your floor could save?
quests.hint: Use everything from this stage: hook, clear problem, connected solution, concrete close.
quests.explanation: A full pitch is the sum of every skill in this stage working together, not any one trick on its own.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Now take the full internet-splitting pitch you just built and deliver it to a landlord instead of a neighbor - someone who cares about fewer complaints and less admin, not personal savings.
quests.correctAnswer: Tenants sharing one connection means one bill for the building instead of five separate accounts to field complaints about - less hassle for you, and residents who are happier with their setup.
quests.hint: Rebuild the message around the landlord's actual priority, not the tenant's savings.
quests.explanation: Finishing Stage One means you can take one true idea and reshape it convincingly for a completely different listener, on demand.
